items.description: Dans son projet de loi de finances 2027, Sébastien Lecornu entend rogner le budget alloué au soutien des pays démunis ou émergents d’1,85 milliards d’euros. Une énième taille en totale contradiction avec les récentes envolées lyriques de Macron sur le multilatéralisme.

items.title: How Iran surprised the world?
items.description: TEHRAN - Russian President Vladimir Putin is not alone in saying that Iran’s resilience in the war with the United States and Israel has surprised the world. From a former head of Britain’s MI6 to senior American analysts, politicians and major international think tanks, a recurring assessment has emerged during the conflict: Iran proved considerably more resilient than many in Washington and Tel Aviv had anticipated.

items.title: Ethiopia accuses Sudan of backing opposition, reshuffled hope for Idris’s govt, tribal violence engulfs South Darfur, military opens road to West Kordofan, China on Sudan’s coast
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . Sudan’s government is taking a long hard look in the mirror, and they don’t like what they see, sources close to Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the Transitional Sovereignty Council told Mada Masr this week. Ushered in on a promise of hope a year ago, Idris’s government has faced significant issues. Some of those come down to war-time trials, but infighting and attempts to delimit the remit of a civilian government backed by a powerful and intrusive military council have been persistent issues. Now the government is considering a reshuffle of ministerial and gubernatorial appointments to address executive imbalances and shortfalls, particularly on economic and service-related issues, according to a source in Idris’s office. While Idris and the TSC may see an administrative reshuffle as a way to address war-time woes, the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement insist that any bureaucratic rearrangement must not change the power-sharing agreement inked in the South Sudanese capital. For now, the reshuffle is all just talk. But the movements do not view it in isolation from the larger reshaping of the political landscape of recent months, a leader in one of the Juba armed movements told Mada Masr, particularly as the planned national dialogue will have to address their relationship with the government. Outside military-controlled areas, the Rapid Support Forces have also been dealing with internal discord over the last two weeks, though the dispute they are presiding over has a decidedly less understanding and diplomatic tenor. Throughout September, deadly inter-tribal clashes have engulfed South Darfur. With heavy weapons in hand and grappling with a faltering rainy season, tribes in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, and in southern parts of Nyala itself, have become embroiled in violent confrontations. The RSF has tried to step in to calm the situation, deploying troops to prevent it from continuing to spiral out of control. As residents look on to see how effective these immediate tamping down measures will be, civil society and RSF sources agree that the much more difficult problem will be halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential communities, which allows competition over water, pasture and farmland during droughts to become increasingly militarized. On Sudan’s battlefields this week, the military cleared the last major RSF defensive positions in North Kordofan, effectively opening the West Kordofan front. These losses have triggered yet another defection from the paramilitary group, as Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed arrived to Omdurman, saying he left after witnessing “tragedies” and “collapse” within the RSF’s ranks. But while frontline battles remain consequential, drone warfare continues to figure in Sudan’s conflict. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed. This week also saw a series of tense diplomatic exchanges. The first came at the UN General Assembly’s debate on Monday, with the United Arab Emirates and Sudanese delegations engaging in tug-of-war over the narrative on Sudan’s conflict. A former official said the spat does not necessarily signal another diplomatic rupture. But the second tense diplomatic moment could prove more consequential. Ethiopia, recently plunged into another civil war, accused Sudan of abetting opposition fighters then took the more drastic diplomatic step of expelling Eritrean and Egyptian diplomats. While wars and their fallout dominate the headlines this week, Sudan is taking steps toward a post-war future. And as with previous attempts to attract foreign powers to Khartoum, this future projection involves lucrative real estate on Sudan’s Red Sea coast. But instead of Russia or the UAE, this time, it is China that is coming in to revive the Abu Amama port project, two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with an Emirati-led consortium to execute the project. *** After TSC review, Idris prepares for govt reshuffle, Juba armed movements to join talks Prime Minister Kamel Idris and the members of the “Government of Hope.” Courtesy: The Government of Hope. Prime Minister Kamel Idris has begun holding consultations in recent days in preparation for reshuffling his government just over a year after it was formed, sources close to the premiership and the TSC told Mada Masr. The talks, which sources said cover several ministries and state governorships, follow an earlier decree ordering a review of government appointments made in recent months, which alarmed the armed movements that signed the 2020 Juba peace agreement over fears that their guaranteed share of executive power under the terms of the deal could be reconsidered. The ministries under review are mostly economy- and service-focused, while governors are being judged largely on how they have restored services in military-recaptured states. The final lineup is yet to be agreed. The reshuffle would be the first major review of the “Government of Hope” since it was completed last summer and is expected to affect ministries held by the armed movements, chiefly the Finance Ministry, the sources said. The movements’ positions in the government were themselves secured under political pressure. Idris had initially proposed a cabinet of non-partisan technocrats, but after months of deadlock, the TSC intervened and pushed him to preserve the movements’ positions under the peace agreement. A year later, the TSC is again directly involved, this time in monitoring and assessing the performance of ministries, including some of those held by the same movements it had helped keep in government. The review comes as Khartoum is still trying to turn military gains into evidence of a functioning state. Over the past year and a half, the government has brought millions of Sudanese back to areas recaptured by the military under a “ voluntary return ” campaign, promising that institutions and basic services would follow. But war-related needs continue to consume public money. The pound is collapsing, while the productive sectors that might replenish the treasury with domestic income or foreign currency remain badly damaged or outside government control. Across the areas where people have returned, basic infrastructure is still damaged. The reshuffle is a review of who is responsible for managing that gap. According to a source in Idris’s office, the changes are aimed at addressing what the government sees as imbalances and shortcomings in the performance of the executive branch, particularly on economic and service-related issues. The Finance Ministry is therefore among the portfolios under particular scrutiny, the source said. It is held by Gibril Ibrahim, the leader of the Justice and Equality Movement and the longest-serving finance minister in Sudan’s history. His Cabinet position was itself the product of the political settlement the TSC pressed Idris to accept. So far, the reshuffle remains a set of negotiations rather than a settled list of departures. No final decisions have been made on which ministers will leave or who will replace them, according to the source in Idris’s office and a source informed of the talks. Idris is approaching the process as a reorganization of the executive branch rather than a wholesale change of government, the source in the prime minister’s office said, with some ministers expected to stay on to complete work already underway and others potentially moving or getting replaced over performance problems or overlapping responsibilities. According to the source informed of the consultations, the health and digital transformation and communications portfolios are not expected to change. The rest are being assessed before a final lineup is agreed, with both political considerations and the performance of the ministries in question taken into account, the source said, citing information available to him. The Juba movements are part of those negotiations. Their representatives hold several of the ministries under review, and consultations with them are a central part of the process, he added. The movements’ 25-percent share of executive power remains in place, the source stressed, meaning changes to individual ministers do not necessarily reopen the quota itself. The movements currently hold several ministries, including finance, human resources and social welfare, federal governance, minerals, and infrastructure and transport. Still, the movements are watching the reshuffle against a broader political landscape that is already in flux. A JEM leader told Mada Masr that the movement and other Juba signatories continue to regard the peace agreement as the framework for their participation in government. Any change to that arrangement, he said, would have to be discussed among the parties to the agreement. JEM does not object to reviewing ministries or changing ministers, he said, provided that the changes are based on performance and the need to improve the government’s work, and are made in consultation with the movements. That worry is unfolding as Khartoum moves toward an internal dialogue over the shape of the transitional period. The movements do not see the reshuffle as separate from that process, the leader said, because the coming political discussions will also have to address the relationship between the government and the armed movements. Their participation, he added, should not be reduced to a question of who holds which ministry. The push for a reshuffle did not begin entirely inside the prime minister’s office. The TSC spent a period monitoring the government’s performance and discussing its findings with Idris, according to a source close to TSC Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan. TSC member Ibrahim Gaber followed ministries tied to production and the economy, while TSC member Shams Eddin Kabbashi monitored other executive portfolios, the source said. Their assessment identified persistent problems with production, revenues and public services and pointed to a need to reorganize some portfolios and replace officials in specific positions. Those findings are now feeding into the reshuffle, including the discussions over the Finance Ministry, as the government grapples with mounting economic pressures. The question of who will hold the ministry is being considered alongside the broader review, the source said. The TSC’s interference is itself part of the questions the reshuffle is meant to address. The source close to Burhan rejected the idea that the TSC was taking over the government, saying its monitoring was part of following priority files during the war and amid diminishing public resources. In practice, however, the boundary has remained blurred since the government’s formation. The attempt to give the executive branch a civilian face has never resolved the military leadership’s role in governing it. The TSC’s discussions with Idris following its review covered the government’s ability to implement decisions, relations between federal ministries and states and overlapping responsibilities among government bodies, the source close to Burhan said. A source close to the prime minister said the first government left unresolved the relationship between ministers from the armed movements and Idris’s executive program, the extent to which the TSC would be willing to step back from running executive affairs and the division of responsibilities between the federal government and the states. Those questions are now on the table as part of the reshuffle talks, the source added. The reshuffle is also expected to extend beyond the federal cabinet to the state governorships, with Khartoum emerging as a particular focus of the discussions, according to the source close to Burhan. The capital has become the clearest test of the government’s ability to restore basic services after the war. Federal institutions moved back to Khartoum in January, but the city’s infrastructure remains badly damaged. Electricity and water networks, roads, bridges, government buildings and health facilities all require repair, while unexploded ordnance and other remnants of the fighting continue to obstruct access and delay restoration work. The return of the government has also come alongside the return of large numbers of residents, who moved into areas relatively less damaged by the war, thus putting extreme pressure on infrastructure meant to serve a smaller population. Parts of Khartoum, Bahri and Omdurman, the three cities that make up the capital, continue to face severe shortages of services, while the reopening of markets and public institutions has remained uneven. That has made the management of the return an important part of the discussion over the governors. The source close to Burhan said several governors could be replaced, with particular attention on Khartoum State. Their performance is expected to be assessed in part on their ability to manage the return of residents, restore services and revive economic activity. Any changes to the governors are expected to accompany the federal reshuffle, with responsibilities between the center and the states potentially redistributed according to their ability to implement reconstruction and service restoration programs, according to the source informed of the consultations. Names have been proposed for some positions, but Idris has yet to make final decisions. According to the source in his office, Idris wants to complete discussions with the relevant parties before submitting the new lineup for approval. The source close to Burhan said the reshuffle should produce “greater harmony” between the government and the TSC in managing economic and service-related issues in the period ahead. *** Weeks of tribal violence in South Darfur leave communities in precarity Effects of the drought on agricultural land in Sereif, South Darfur, September 23. Courtesy: Darfur Victims Support via X. Heavy weapons in the hands of local groups, weakened controls on the use of force and a failed rainy season have converged to push South Darfur into a month of deadly inter-tribal clashes, including in and around Nyala, the seat of the RSF’s parallel government. At least 16 people were killed and dozens wounded in clashes between Massalit and Fallata communities in Gereida, about 90 km south of Nyala, after a dispute in a market earlier this month escalated into fighting across the town, medical sources and residents told Mada Masr. Hundreds of residents fled, fires broke out in residential areas and in a displacement camp, and the violence later spread to the farmland north of the town, where farmers were also caught up in it. The harvest season brings the two predominantly agricultural communities into close contact in Gereida’s markets, where farmers sell their crops and people from surrounding villages converge, giving rise to frictions. This year, poor rains and a weak harvest have added to the pressures around those interactions, according to a senior RSF source in the office of South Darfur’s governor. The fighting began on September 19 in Abuja market, when a dispute between a Massalit and a Fallata turned violent. Armed men from both sides quickly joined, and the fight spread into nearby neighborhoods, with light and heavy weapons in use, a medical source in Gereida said. Twelve people were killed and dozens wounded that day, according to the source. The town’s health facilities, already limited, took in casualties throughout the fighting. Some of the seriously wounded were taken to Nyala, while others stayed in Gereida because the roads out of town were too dangerous due to the clashes, he said. Tribal administration leaders stepped in to defuse the situation and RSF security personnel intervened overnight to separate the two sides, a police source in Gereida told Mada Masr. The calm lasted only a few hours. On September 20, armed groups attacked from the town’s eastern and western sides, and fighting spread again, the source said. Heavy weapons and Kalashnikov shots could be heard across Gereida, while forces stationed in the town took up positions at its entrances and outskirts to prevent the fighting from spreading further, he added. Four more people were killed and 23 wounded in the renewed clashes, according to a second medical source in Gereida. Some of the casualties were shot inside residential areas, the source said. Local leaders continued working to end the fighting and return the bodies of the dead to their families, said Sulaiman Abdel Rahman, a South Darfur notable. Reinforcements arrived from Buram, south of Gereida, along with civilian protection forces from Nyala, to separate the two sides and prevent another escalation, he said. The two days of fighting displaced residents mainly from western and northern Gereida, where the clashes were concentrated, Abdel Rahman said. Fires also broke out in parts of the Babanusa neighborhood and in the Abyad displacement camp to its east, destroying homes and property. The market stayed closed throughout the fighting, said Ahmed Rizgallah, who lives in Gereida. Movement between the town, surrounding villages and Nyala also stopped as armed personnel took up positions to the north, east and west of the town. The security deployment brought an uneasy calm to Gereida. But it also changed where the violence was taking place. With armed security forces in the town, the fighting moved into the surrounding farmland. On September 21, clashes broke out north of Gereida, where some farmers live and where other residents had sought refuge from the violence in town. Several farmers were killed and wounded, Rizgallah said. Some families who had been staying in the farmland returned to Gereida, while others could not make the journey safely and moved farther away, to places such as Um Dubban and Um Rakouba, he added. A Gereida locality official said a total of 412 people fled the town for areas within the Gereida and Tulus localities. For communities that depend on farming and trade, displacement, the shuttered market and blocked roads mean the damage extends well beyond the immediate violence, a community source added. Community leaders and security forces are working to prevent a new outbreak, but another Gereida resident said people see the situation as liable to flare up again at the slightest friction, with armed men still present in and around the town. The senior RSF source in the governor’s office said that the spread of heavy weapons among local groups, together with the erosion of the controls that once governed the use of force within communities, means that even a minor dispute can quickly escalate into a wide-scale confrontation, faster than the authorities or tribal administration can contain it. The violence in Gereida was preceded by further tribal violence inside Nyala itself. In early September, members of the Salamat said on social media that Shurafa was a subclan of the Salamat. The claim set off an argument online between members of the two groups, according to an official in South Darfur. The dispute soon moved beyond social media. Small groups of Salamat began attacking Shurafa members in the western part of Sereif, southern Nyala, including at coffee shops and other gathering places, according to the residents. The attacks escalated into armed clashes, with both sides using light and heavy weapons. For several days, the violence remained concentrated in western Sereif, where armed groups could move in and out through areas beyond the RSF’s close control, the official explained. That changed on September 16, when the clashes reached eastern Sereif. The fighting spread through Sereif’s residential areas. Homes were burned and looted, and families fled to other parts of the district or stayed indoors as gunfire continued, a resident of Sereif said. At least 10 people were killed and others wounded, the official said. Sereif is divided by Wadi Barly into eastern and western sections. The RSF has a stronger presence in the east, while the west has fluid boundaries that it cannot police closely. When the fighting reached eastern Sereif, the RSF was able to intervene, deploying forces around the affected neighborhoods, according to the official. But the violence flared again the following day as armed men from both sides arrived from outside Sereif, he said. RSF personnel once again separated the two sides and detained around 30 people involved in the clashes, an RSF military source said. The larger clashes have since subsided, but residents told Mada Masr the violence has not fully stopped. Skirmishes continue, particularly in western Sereif, and armed deployments have restricted movement across the area. Many of those who fled have been reluctant to return. One resident said families are waiting to see whether the RSF can keep armed groups from moving back in before deciding whether it is safe to go home. A South Darfur civil society source said in both Nyala and Gereida “weapons were the key factor in turning a limited dispute into a wider confrontation. Security forces in the area only intervened after the fighting had spread.” The senior RSF source said authorities are deeply concerned by the successive clashes, particularly because security and climate pressures are converging during this time. As the drought intensifies competition over water, pasture and farmland, resources that already fuel conflict across Darfur every year, the spread of arms makes it far easier for local disputes to escalate, he said. In his view, an intervention should include halting the spread of heavy weapons into residential and rural areas and swiftly activating the conflict mitigation mechanisms of tribal administration and local authorities before clashes widen and trigger displacement and disrupt the farming season. *** Military captures RSF’s last major defensive positions in western North Kordofan The military captured Mazroub, the RSF’s final major defensive position in western North Kordofan, on Friday morning after what it described as fierce battles, opening the way toward northern West Kordofan. The military had imposed a three-sided siege on Mazroub over the past week, after retaking nearby Sodary on September 25, according to a military source and a former officer who spoke to Mada Masr before the fall of Mazroub. The RSF had been preparing for a direct assault on Mazroub, concentrating troops and vehicles there. Instead, the military moved on Sodary first. When the town fell, the RSF was left defending Mazroub with fewer options for movement, the former officer said. The RSF subsequently reinforced Mazroub, sending additional troops and vehicles on Saturday that took up positions to its west, a second military source said. According to the first military source, the group had recognized that losing Mazroub would effectively end its presence in North Kordofan, while also threatening its positions in northern West Kordofan and its remaining defensive line across the wider Kordofan region. The capture of Sodary followed heavy fighting that caused significant losses to the RSF in personnel and equipment, the source said. Their remaining forces withdrew west toward Um Bader and from there, south toward Wad Banda in West Kordofan, while military and allied forces continued advancing toward Um Shuru, southwest of Sodary. The town is strategic because it sits along routes linking North Kordofan with West Kordofan and North Darfur, including the Arbaeen Road, the desert route connecting the two regions. Its capture helps the military further secure the Saderat Road, which runs through North Kordofan from North Darfur toward Omdurman, as well as areas retaken by the military over the past months. Mohamed Didan, the spokesperson for the military’s special operations forces in West Kordofan, said the loss of Sodary would disrupt RSF supply lines and leave its remaining forces in northern North Kordofan increasingly isolated. According to the former official, the military’s broader advance in North Kordofan is taking place along three axes: west from Sodary toward Abu Zaeima, Hamra al-Sheikh and Um Bader; from west of Bara toward Mazroub and Um Kiredam; and from west of Obeid toward Khawi and Nuhud in West Kordofan. The western Obeid axis had previously been a risky route for the military. The RSF surrounded the area from three sides, leaving any advancing force exposed in a confined battlefield where it could be vulnerable to ambushes, the former officer said. Sodary’s capture changes that position. And with Mazroub now in the military’s hands, the RSF would face pressure from several directions while its supply routes are cut. The resulting pressure could force the group to withdraw from towns and areas in northern West Kordofan, particularly because, he said, the RSF has less experience holding positions under siege. *** RSF launches drone attacks on Obeid, Wad Madani Aftermath of an RSF drone strike on the University of Kordofan’s dormitory in Obeid, North Kordofan, October 1. Courtesy: Sudan Tribune via X. RSF drones struck targets in Gezira and North Kordofan over the week, reaching fuel infrastructure east of Wad Madani and multiple sites in Obeid, where at least six civilians were killed. In Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, more than 15 drones struck different parts of the city on Thursday, including a shelter at the University of Kordofan’s dormitory, a security source told Mada Masr. He said the drones were launched from RSF-held Ghubeish in West Kordofan. The Sudan Doctors Network said the attacks killed five people and wounded 47 others. The Thursday attacks followed strikes on other parts of Obeid earlier in the week. The Olympic Stadium in the northern Wadi Elias neighborhood was struck on Monday, followed by an attack with three suicide drones on an events hall in the city on Tuesday evening, a state official told Mada Masr. The United Nations said at least one civilian was killed. An activist in Obeid told Mada Masr that the military had been using the stadium as a military facility since the start of the war. The strike triggered an explosion at an ammunition and weapons depot inside it, he added. Several buildings near the stadium were damaged, including the Sheikan College, according to the official. The drone attacks had reached Gezira on Sunday, targeting fuel storage facilities in Um Alila, east of the state capital, Wad Madani, according to a police-affiliated field source. The drones hit fuel tankers at the site, triggering a large fire and sending columns of smoke into the sky, the source said. The facilities are among the main fuel storage sites serving Gezira and central Sudan. Three other drones crashed before exploding in agricultural fields in the village of Wad al-Bar al-Khawalda, in the Wad Raeya administrative unit, he added. The following day, Gezira’s state security committee, headed by Governor Al-Taher Ibrahim, inspected the fuel facility and said the damage was limited, adding that it would resume operations within days. *** RSF unit from North Kordofan defects to military A force of 50 RSF fighters under the command of Al-Tayeb “Waheedo” Mohamed Ahmed announced its defection on September 25, marking the third such breakaway from the paramilitary group in Kordofan in recent months. According to a military source who spoke to Mada Masr, the force arrived from the North Kordofan battlefronts in Omdurman, where Waheedo was received alongside several military commanders and members of a committee responsible for coordinating the affairs of RSF defectors. In his first statements to the press, Waheedo said he left the RSF after witnessing the “tragedies” and “collapse” within its ranks. He called on those still fighting with the group to follow suit. The latest defection follows the arrival in September of 200 RSF fighters under Abu Bakr Dahloub , the group’s intelligence chief for special missions in North Kordofan’s Hamra al-Sheikh and the Egypt-Libya-Sudan border triangle. In July, RSF field commander Hussein al-Dodo defected with 280 fighters. He had commanded one of the RSF’s units in Bara. *** Sudan rejects Ethiopian accusations of backing armed opposition As fighting escalates across three northern Ethiopian regions between the federal military and armed opposition groups, the Sudanese military and Foreign Ministry have rejected accusations from Addis Ababa that Khartoum is supporting Ethiopian opposition armed factions. In a video statement on September 25, Ethiopian National Defense Force Chief of General Staff Birhanu Jula accused Eritrea of acting as an intermediary between external powers and the newly formed alliance of armed groups in an effort to destabilize and weaken Ethiopia, saying the current security challenges were part of a broader strategy by what he described as the country’s “historical” and “contemporary” adversaries. “Neither Eritrea nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front can achieve anything on their own, even if they are allied, unless they are backed, supported and supplied by Sudan, Egypt and other external powers,” he said. The statement came days after the TPLF declared a “defensive war” against the Ethiopian government, as clashes between federal forces and a newly formed opposition alliance, the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival , spread across Tigray, which borders Sudan and Eritrea, and into the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. The Sudanese military rejected the accusations on Sunday, calling them “baseless” and saying Sudan respects international law, the principles of good neighborly relations and the sovereignty of other countries. It also turned the accusation back on Ethiopia, saying it has information and evidence that the RSF continues to receive support via Ethiopia, including training and supplies, and that Ethiopian territory is being used for military activities, including drone operations. The military called on Ethiopia to exercise accuracy and responsibility and to address such issues through dialogue and official channels. The day after, the Sudanese government reinforced the military’s response through the Foreign Ministry, which also rejected the accusations, describing them as “arbitrary” and saying they had “no basis or evidence.” The ministry said the Ethiopian military chief’s remarks were an attempt to “drag Sudan into the internal conflicts engulfing Ethiopia.” From Khartoum’s perspective, the significance of the Ethiopian statements goes beyond the direct accusation that Sudan is supporting the Tigray front, a Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr. The source said the statements came as the Ethiopian government seeks to explain the emergence of a new military alignment inside the country as the result of outside interference, rather than as a development rooted in Ethiopia’s own political and security crisis. Bringing Sudan, Egypt and Eritrea into that narrative gives Addis Ababa a regional frame for the conflict, the source said. Khartoum is wary of that framing because it could turn the Sudan-Ethiopia border, already marked by longstanding territorial and security disputes, into another arena of Ethiopia’s internal conflict, the source said. Sudan wants to maintain its stated position that its territory will not be used as a launchpad for activities targeting neighboring countries, he added, while retaining the right to respond to any activity it considers a threat to its security. The military shares the immediate concern of a spillover, according to a Sudanese military source informed of the assessments of Sudan’s General Command. As the fighting expands, Ethiopia’s western border with Sudan is increasingly becoming part of the conflict’s military calculations, the source told Mada Masr. The military also sees the accusation itself as an attempt to redirect attention from the support the RSF receives from Ethiopia and toward a Sudanese role in Ethiopia’s internal conflict, he added. Any claim that Sudan is supporting Ethiopian armed factions, the source stressed, should be accompanied by specific evidence from the ground, something Addis Ababa has not provided in the statements made by its military chief. On Thursday, the Ethiopian Foreign Ministry announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital of Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats in Addis Ababa persona non grata, ordering them to leave within 48 hours. The ministry said the step was “in response to Eritrea’s direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia.” The move marks one of the sharpest diplomatic escalations between the two countries since they restored relations in 2018. Asmara responded later in the day by announcing it had severed all diplomatic ties with Addis Ababa, citing what it described as “Ethiopia’s deplorable acts of hostility.” Addis Ababa also took action against Cairo on Thursday afternoon, declaring a member of the Egyptian diplomatic mission in Ethiopia persona non grata and ordering him to leave within 48 hours. Egypt responded in kind, expelling the Ethiopian embassy’s advisor in Cairo. *** Sudanese-Emirati war of words at UN General Assembly Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem during his speech at the UN General Assembly, 28 September. Courtesy: The UN. The Sudanese and Emirati delegations took the floor one after the other at the UN General Assembly’s debate on Monday, setting out competing visions for an end to Sudan’s war, before turning on each other in two rounds of increasingly heated exchanges after the general debate concluded. Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohie Eddin Salem opened by expressing regret that he was the one addressing the General Assembly, rather than Transitional Sovereignty Council and Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, whose United States visa was denied. Salem called for “comprehensive, equitable and expeditious reform of the international system” and urged countries to refrain from “the use of force or the threat thereof in international relations” and from imposing coercive measures on the basis of political disagreements. The visa denial has been read within Sudanese official circles as an attempt to pressure the government over its resistance to a truce proposal Washington is now pushing, Sudanese officials told Mada Masr last week. Salem said the government “categorically rejects any attempt to impose external solutions, dictates or agendas on our people.” The Sudanese people, he said, “should determine their own future without influence or pressure.” Khartoum, he said, has begun its own political process that will lead to free and fair elections. Then the UAE took the floor. On Sudan, Minister of State at the Emirati Foreign Ministry Khalifa Shaheen al-Marar said his country has stressed the need to “end the humanitarian catastrophe,” and called for “a permanent and unconditional ceasefire that would bring an end to the civil war,” followed by “a comprehensive and credible political process led by civilians.” The resulting government, he said, should be independent of both parties to the conflict and extremist groups. “The future of Sudan must be decided solely by the Sudanese people,” Marar said, calling on the international community to press the “leaders of the Port Sudan authorities” and the RSF, as parties to the conflict, to engage seriously with international initiatives. Sudan exercised its right to reply. Its representative, Al-Harith Idriss , accused the UAE of contributing to the humanitarian catastrophe Marar had referenced “through continuous support to the terrorist militia,” referring to the RSF. The UAE’s “claim to be neutral and innocent,” Idriss said, “will not aid in covering their crimes and their atrocities where they are in a bloodied partnership with the RSF.” He went on to cite evidence of Emirati support for the RSF, including financing, training and military supplies. Idriss also took issue with the UAE’s reference to the Sudanese government as the “Port Sudan authorities,” saying the language was out of place at the UN forum, before turning to a wider attack on Abu Dhabi and its own regime. He also accused the UAE of “leading an international campaign to expand the scope of the arms embargo to target the Sudanese Armed Forces,” referring to the US draft resolution discussed at the Security Council last month that sought to expand the Darfur arms embargo to cover all of Sudan and include Sudanese state institutions. The UAE came back with its own right to reply, accusing the Sudanese military of using chemical weapons and saying it would not “be lectured” by a military government that had committed war crimes against its own population. The two sides went back and forth twice, turning the General Assembly floor into a direct diplomatic confrontation over the war, the legitimacy of Sudan’s government and the role of the UAE. A Sudanese diplomatic source told Mada Masr that the escalation should not necessarily be understood as a step toward another diplomatic rupture. Rather, it reflects how both sides are using international forums to exert pressure and reinforce competing narratives of the war. Khartoum wants the international discussion to focus on foreign support for the RSF and rejects equating the military with the paramilitary force. Abu Dhabi, meanwhile, is pushing for a political process that would keep both sides of the war out of the next government, the source said. Khartoum also rejects the UAE’s role in the international effort to end the war, arguing that Abu Dhabi cannot act as a mediator while being, in Sudan’s view, a party to the conflict. The UAE is part of the US-led Quad on Sudan — alongside Egypt and Saudi Arabia — which has backed several ceasefire proposals rejected by Khartoum. The confrontation at the General Assembly is only the latest chapter in a dispute that has increasingly spilled into international forums since the war began, the source said. Sudan has repeatedly taken its accusations against the UAE to the Security Council and International Criminal Court, while Abu Dhabi has continued to deny them. *** Sudan turns to China for Red Sea port after scrapped UAE deal Two years after Sudan cancelled a memorandum of understanding with a UAE-led consortium to build Sudan’s Abu Amama port , the government is reviving the project with a major Chinese port company, Hassan Gaafar, the deputy head of the state-owned Sea Ports Corporation and head of its Higher Committee for the International Conference on Seaports, told Mada Masr. Sudan has begun taking practical steps toward building the port, Gaafar said. Studies are expected to be completed and construction to begin by the end of 2027, he said. The move is part of a broader expansion of Sudan’s economic ties with China, as the government looks to Beijing for investment in ports, energy and infrastructure, according to Sudanese government and diplomatic sources. China Harbour Engineering Company signed an agreement with Sudan in July to develop existing ports and build new ones, while other Chinese companies are in talks over electricity and infrastructure projects, a Foreign Ministry source said. Abu Amama lies about 200 km north of Port Sudan, near the Mohamed Qol and Marsa Oseif port localities, along the Red Sea coast and close to major shipping routes. The area has deep waters, reducing the need for extensive dredging and allowing it to accommodate large vessels and cargo ships. The details of the proposed arrangement with China, including financing, the length of any concession and who would operate the port, have yet to be formally announced. The Chinese-backed version of the project is being developed as part of a different government approach to Sudan’s ports, according to a Finance Ministry source informed of the ports file. Rather than being part of a single, large investment package, Abu Amama is now being presented as part of a government push to expand Sudan’s port capacity and improve its ability to move imports and exports. The government is exploring an investment model that would link the port more closely to Sudanese trade and exports, the source said. The UAE deal, signed in December 2022, was considerably broader. Under the agreement, a consortium comprising AD Ports Group and Invictus Investment was to develop, operate and manage Abu Amama, with announced investments of up to US$6 billion. The package included a free trade zone, an agricultural project and a $300 million deposit at the Central Bank of Sudan, according to the Sudanese government announcement at the time. For the UAE investors, Abu Amama’s location was a central part of the appeal, the Finance Ministry source said. The port could serve as an outlet for Sudanese exports and imports and connect the coast to agricultural and mining production areas and overland transport networks, he added. The project would have given Sudan another port alongside the Port Sudan complex, while giving the UAE-led consortium a long-term role in developing and operating a facility on a major global shipping route, the source said. The government cancelled the agreement in November 2024, as relations between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi deteriorated after Sudan accused the UAE of backing the RSF in the war. At the time, Finance Minister and JEM leader Gibril Ibrahim told reporters that, following the UAE’s support for the RSF, “there is no [Sudanese] entity that could even think about giving a port to the UAE, not even a single centimeter of land.” A Sudanese government source told Mada Masr that the cancellation was part of a broader reassessment of the country’s economic relationship with the UAE since the war. Ports, the source said, have since become part of Sudan’s political and security calculations in its foreign relations, alongside their role as commercial infrastructure. A diplomatic source informed of Sudan-UAE relations said Abu Dhabi may view the transfer of Abu Amama to a Chinese partner as part of Sudan’s wider economic realignment following the political crisis between the two countries. The main question for the UAE, the source said, would be whether the new arrangement will reproduce any of the rights granted to the UAE-led consortium under the original agreement, including long-term operating rights or ownership of related assets. The project comes as Sudan’s economic ties with China expand. Chinese cooperation has increasingly extended into infrastructure, energy and ports in recent months, while Sudan is looking for long-term investment to rebuild infrastructure damaged by the war and sees its ports as a key route back into foreign trade, a Sudanese diplomatic source and the government source said. Under the potential Chinese model, the first phase could focus on building the port’s basic infrastructure, followed by expanding its operating capacity and connecting it to transport networks and areas producing goods for export, the government source said. But much of the project’s success will depend on what happens beyond the port itself. A maritime transport expert told Mada Masr that Abu Amama could ease pressure on existing facilities if it were connected to roads and railways capable of moving goods from production areas to the coast. Its economic viability would depend not only on the depth of the water, the expert said, but also on the cost of building berths, container terminals, warehouses and logistics zones, as well as the transport links connecting the port to Sudan’s interior. The port could handle agricultural exports, livestock, minerals and imports, but serving those markets would require a logistics network extending well beyond the construction of the quay itself, the expert said. That broader challenge is part of why the government is looking at the ports sector as a pillar of post-war economic reconstruction. The International Conference on Sudanese Ports opened in Port Sudan on September 27, bringing together experts and institutions from Sudan, China, Egypt, Spain and Norway to discuss investment, infrastructure, supply chains, digital transformation and public-private partnerships. A government official participating in the conference told Mada Masr that Sudan wants to move away from reliance on its existing ports toward a more diversified network along the Red Sea, combining the expansion of current facilities with new ports capable of handling trade. Reviving Abu Amama with a Chinese partner is part of that effort, the official said, allowing Sudan to draw on Chinese experience in building and operating maritime infrastructure. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . items.title: Ferran Torres quitte le rassemblement de la sélection espagnole
items.description: L’attaquant du Paris SG Ferran Torres, touché à la cheville gauche, va quitter le rassemblement de la sélection espagnole et rentrer en France pour se soigner, a annoncé vendredi la Fédération espagnole de football. La RFEF a précisé dans un communiqué avoir libéré le nouveau buteur parisien, qui souffrait depuis plusieurs jours de douleurs à la cheville gauche, pour « prioriser sa récupération ». Torres, auteur du but vainqueur en finale du Mondial-2026 cet été, sera remplacé par le jeune attaquant du Real Madrid Carlos Espi pour les deux prochains matches de Ligue des nations contre la République tchèque et la Croatie. Pour éviter un potentiel conflit, la Fédération espagnole assure que ses médecins sont « restés en contact permanent » avec les services médicaux du PSG depuis le début de la trêve internationale. L’attaquant de 26 ans, auteur d’un excellent début de saison avec Paris (4 buts), va rentrer en France pour effectuer des examens complémentaires, a confirmé la RFEF à l’AFP. The post Ferran Torres quitte le rassemblement de la sélection espagnole appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Commercialisation de produits SOFTCARE au Sénégal : les députés examinent le rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire
items.description: La séance plénière de l’Assemblée nationale, tenue ce vendredi 2 octobre 2026, a été consacrée à l’examen du rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire relative à la commercialisation des produits de marque SOFTCARE au Sénégal. Les députés ont ouvert une plénière vendredi, pour examiner le rapport de la Mission d’information parlementaire relative à la commercialisation des produits de marque SOFTCARE au Sénégal. Instituée en application de l’article 51 du Règlement intérieur de l’Assemblée nationale, cette Mission, mise en place à l’initiative de la Commission de la Santé, de la Population, des Affaires sociales et de la Solidarité nationale, avait pour objectif d’établir de manière « impartiale, contradictoire et documentée », explique une note de l’Hémicycle, les faits relatifs aux décisions successives de retrait puis de remise sur le marché des produits SOFTCARE. A lire aussi : Affaire Softcare : une mission d’information parlementaire officiellement installée « Installée le 5 décembre 2025, la Mission a mené ses travaux jusqu’au 2 avril 2026. Elle a conduit 20 auditions et effectué une visite de terrain sur le site industriel de SOFTCARE à Sindia, en auditionnant notamment les responsables de l’Agence sénégalaise de Réglementation pharmaceutique (ARP), les représentants de l’entreprise, les administrations concernées, les organisations professionnelles, les associations de consommateurs ainsi que des experts », renseigne le texte. En fait, les travaux ont bénéficié de l’appui technique de la Direction des Services de Planification, de Contrôle et d’Évaluation des politiques publiques (DSPCEPP) et des assistants parlementaires, notamment pour la collecte et l’analyse documentaire, la préparation des auditions et la consolidation des constats. Plusieurs insuffisances relevées dans le rapport Selon la note de l’Assemblée nationale, le rapport relève plusieurs insuffisances techniques, administratives et institutionnelles. Ceci, notamment en matière de traçabilité des matières premières, de gestion des non-conformités, de coordination entre services et de cohérence de la communication institutionnelle. « La Mission constate que des matières premières périmées ont bien été identifiées sur le site de SOFTCARE. Toutefois, au regard des éléments matériels et documentaires disponibles, elle estime qu’il n’est pas possible, à ce stade, d’établir avec certitude leur utilisation dans le processus de fabrication des produits finis », rapporte l’Hémicycle. Renforcer durablement le dispositif de régulation et de contrôle des produits de santé Au-delà du cas SOFTCARE, le rapport met ainsi en évidence la nécessité de renforcer durablement le dispositif de régulation et de contrôle des produits de santé, cosmétiques et d’hygiène. Parmi les recommandations formulées figurent notamment l’achèvement du cadre réglementaire, le renforcement des pouvoirs d’inspection, la modernisation des systèmes de traçabilité, l’amélioration de la coordination interinstitutionnelle, le renforcement des capacités scientifiques et la mise en place d’un suivi parlementaire régulier des réformes engagées. À travers l’examen de ce rapport, l’Assemblée nationale réaffirme ainsi sa volonté d’exercer pleinement sa mission constitutionnelle de contrôle de l’action gouvernementale, dans une démarche fondée sur la rigueur, la transparence, la redevabilité et l’évaluation des politiques publiques. Mariama DIEME

KGL Foundation commits $200,000 to support juvenile football for the next two years
items.description: The KGL Foundation has announced a commitment of $200,000 to the Ghana Football Association (GFA) as part of its support for juvenile football. The financial commitment is set to last for the next two years, starting with the launch of the 2026 KGL U-17 Inter-regional Colts Championship. The launch of the Colts tournament took place in the Conference Room of the KGL House in Labone, Accra, with key stakeholders present. President Kurt Edwin Simeon-Okraku, Executive Council Members, and top officials of the KGL Foundation were all in attendance. The initiative, which was first launched in 2021, has been the bedrock to unlocking young talents in Ghana and giving them the platform to display their potential. Speaking at the launch on Friday, Okraku lauded KGL for their continuous support towards the development of young talents. “We are here to reaffirm the marriage between the Ghana Football Association and the KGL Foundation,” he said. “Over a six-year tenure, we have produced amazing talents not only for local clubs but also for our various youth national teams. Today, I am proud to say that a lot of the products from these championships have represented Ghana at the U-17 level on the international stage, courtesy of the KGL Foundation.” The championship is also aimed at promoting talent discovery, fostering regional unity, supporting youth development, and nurturing future stars from the district level to the national phase. This year, KGL will provide each participating team with 60 kits (30 home jerseys and 30 away jerseys). The teams will also receive footballs, bibs and cones. As part of efforts this year, KGL will also provide educational scholarships to some of the best players from the competition. Ashanti Region were crowned champions for the second time last year following a 2-1 victory over Western Region.

items.title: Poutine assiste aux manœuvres «Centre-2026» et met l’accent sur la préparation, les nouveaux armements et la coopération militaire
items.description: Vladimir Poutine s'est rendu le 2 octobre sur le polygone militaire de Tchebarkoul, dans la region de Tcheliabinsk, ou il a suivi la phase finale des exercices strategiques « Centre-2026 » et des manœuvres « Interaction-2026 », organisees dans le cadre de l'Organisation du traite de securite collective. Ce polygone est un vaste terrain d'entraînement militaire ou les soldats peuvent s'exercer avec differents types d'armements, notamment des armes legeres, de l'artillerie, des systemes de roquettes, des missiles et des moyens aeriens. Prevus par le programme de preparation des forces armees russes, les exercices « Centre-2026 » constituent un dispositif strategique de commandement et d'etat-major. Ils servent notamment a entraîner les responsables militaires et les etats-majors a diriger de grandes formations de troupes dans differents scenarios operationnels. Lances le 28 septembre et prevus jusqu'au 3 octobre, ils se deroulent en deux etapes et mobilisent plus de 47 000 militaires sur onze polygones ainsi que dans les eaux de la mer Caspienne. Plus de 2 000 equipements et systemes d'armes sont engages, dont 90 appareils aeriens et 77 navires de combat ou de soutien. a Tchebarkoul, Vladimir Poutine a observe les manœuvres depuis un point de commandement, pris connaissance des rapports militaires et examine plusieurs modeles d'armements, de drones et de systemes robotises. Il s'est egalement entretenu avec des attaches militaires etrangers presents sur le site. Renforcer la preparation face aux menaces exterieures L'un des principaux buts des manœuvres est d'ameliorer les capacites de commandement des etats-majors dans un scenario d'agression exterieure. « L'objectif principal des exercices est d'ameliorer les competences du personnel dirigeant des etats-majors de tous niveaux dans le commandement des troupes lors de la reponse a une agression exterieure », a declare Vladimir Poutine. Le scenario porte notamment sur des operations dans la direction strategique d'Asie centrale ainsi que sur la securite militaire dans la zone de la mer Caspienne. Le president russe a egalement souligne que les participants utilisaient de nouveaux armements et equipements en tenant compte, selon ses termes, de l'experience acquise dans le cadre de l'« operation militaire speciale ». Cette experience est ainsi integree a la preparation des unites et aux differentes sequences des manœuvres. Le vice-ministre russe de la Defense Iounous-Bek Evkourov a presente a Vladimir Poutine le deroulement du scenario simule et les differentes phases de l'exercice. Les exercices « Centre-2026 » sont menes parallelement a « Interaction-2026 ». Ce dernier est un exercice de commandement mene dans le cadre de l'OTSC, qui associe notamment des unites de plusieurs etats membres de l'organisation. Les deux series de manœuvres se deroulent dans une meme situation operationnelle afin de travailler la coordination entre les forces participantes. Une cooperation militaire elargie avec les partenaires La participation internationale constitue un autre volet important des exercices. Des representants de 41 etats y prennent part sous differentes formes, un niveau de participation presente comme inedit pour « Centre-2026 ». La Bielorussie, la Chine, le Kirghizstan, la Mongolie, le Pakistan et le Tadjikistan ont envoye des contingents militaires. Le Kazakhstan et le Congo participent avec des groupes operationnels, tandis que 33 etats sont representes en qualite d'observateurs. Cette presence etrangere accompagne les manœuvres conduites dans le cadre de l'OTSC et les differentes sequences de cooperation entre les forces participantes. a l'issue des exercices, Vladimir Poutine a mis l'accent sur l'importance des echanges entre militaires de differents pays. Il a estime que ces echanges renforcaient la confiance entre les armees participantes. « Quand les militaires communiquent entre eux, cela signifie que la confiance se renforce entre les militaires et entre les etats qu'ils representent », a declare le president russe. Il s'est egalement dit convaincu que l'experience acquise pendant « Centre-2026 » et « Interaction-2026 » permettrait d'ameliorer l'efficacite de la reponse des forces participantes.

items.title: Labé : le 68ᵉ anniversaire de l’indépendance célébré sous le signe de la citoyenneté et de l’engagement
items.description: La cérémonie de célébration du 68ᵉ anniversaire de l’indépendance de la Guinée s’est tenue ce vendredi à la Place des Martyrs de Labé, en présence des autorités administratives et communales, des sages, des jeunes, des femmes, des forces de défense et de sécurité, ainsi que de plusieurs acteurs de la société civile. Depuis le 25 septembre, la ville de Labé vit au rythme de la Semaine de l’indépendance, marquée par diverses activités citoyennes, notamment des opérations d’assainissement et d’embellissement de la ville. Dans son intervention, le maire de la commune urbaine de Labé, Mamadou Habibou Bah, a salué l’implication des différentes composantes de la population dans les activités organisées à l’occasion de cette célébration. « Depuis le 25 septembre, Labé vit au rythme de la semaine de l’indépendance. Durant ces jours de célébration, notre ville s’est unie. Ensemble, nous avons nettoyé et embelli notre ville. Mais surtout, ensemble, nous avons fait vivre la citoyenneté », a-t-il déclaré. Prenant la parole à son tour, le préfet de Labé, le contrôleur général Mohamed Cheick Keita, a rappelé la portée historique de l’indépendance, proclamée le 2 octobre 1958. Il a également invité la jeunesse à contribuer davantage au développement du pays. « Chers jeunes de Labé, vous devez transformer l’héritage de nos aînés en victoire économique, scientifique et culturelle », a-t-il lancé, avant d’appeler les citoyens à « chérir et défendre les symboles républicains ». Pour l’historien Pr Bonata Dieng, cette célébration constitue un moment important pour rappeler le chemin parcouru par la Guinée depuis son accession à l’indépendance. « La Guinée a été un pays qui a osé braver toutes les difficultés et qui aujourd’hui se construit petit à petit. Je demande à la population que chacun soit un acteur du développement », a-t-il souligné. La cérémonie s’est achevée dans une atmosphère marquée par la fierté nationale, avec des appels à renforcer la citoyenneté et l’engagement de chacun en faveur du développement de la Guinée. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Labé : le 68ᵉ anniversaire de l’indépendance célébré sous le signe de la citoyenneté et de l’engagement est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: La Guinée célèbre le 68ᵉ anniversaire de son indépendance
items.description: La Republique de Guinee celebre ce 2 octobre le 68ᵉ anniversaire de son independance du joug colonial francais, proclamee en 1958. Quelques semaines auparavant, le general Charles de Gaulle s'etait rendu a Conakry dans le cadre d'une tournee africaine destinee a presenter le projet de nouvelle Constitution francaise et la Communaute appelee a remplacer l'Union francaise. Le 25 août 1958, il avait notamment rencontre les principales figures politiques du territoire, parmi lesquelles Saifoulaye Diallo, president de l'Assemblee territoriale, et Sekou Toure, president du Conseil de gouvernement. C'est au cours de cette visite que Sekou Toure prononca devant De Gaulle son celebre discours defendant le droit des peuples africains a disposer d'eux-memes et affirmant la volonte de la Guinee de choisir librement son avenir. 🇬🇳 AN68 : Célébration de la fête Nationale guinéenne : le président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA procède au dépôt de gerbe de fleurs à la Place des Martyrs. #GN68 #GN67 #GN66 #GN65 #Jeune #SimandouAcademy #Simandou2040 pic.twitter.com/yNGHOTmZsJ — Lamine BA ✨️ (@LamineBA_) October 2, 2026 Le « non » guineen du 28 septembre 1958 Un peu plus d'un mois plus tard, le 28 septembre, les electeurs guineens furent appeles a se prononcer sur la nouvelle Constitution francaise. Le « non » recueillit 95,22 % des suffrages exprimes. La Guinee devint ainsi le seul territoire francais d'Afrique subsaharienne a rejeter le projet et, avec lui, l'entree dans la nouvelle Communaute francaise. Ce resultat singularisa profondement Conakry au sein de l'Afrique occidentale francaise et de l'Afrique equatoriale francaise, ou le « oui » s'etait largement impose. Le choix guineen ouvrit alors la voie a une rupture politique immediate avec la puissance coloniale. 🇬🇳 28 septembre 1958 | Le jour où la Guinée a dit « NON » ! 🗳️ Seul territoire d'Afrique francophone à rejeter la Communauté française avec plus de 94 % des voix, la Guinée ouvrait la voie aux indépendances africaines. ⤵️ https://t.co/mXO7sVJHdE #Guinée #Histoire #28Septembre pic.twitter.com/mdGjHCrFqb — Africaguinee.com (@Africaguinee) September 28, 2026 L'independance proclamee le 2 octobre Une fois les resultats du referendum connus, la Republique de Guinee a proclame son independance quelques jours plus tard, le 2 octobre, entamant ainsi une nouvelle etape de son histoire nationale et devenant la premiere colonie francaise d'Afrique de l'Ouest a acquerir sa souverainete. a la suite de la proclamation de l'independance, la France a retire son aide financiere et technique ainsi que son personnel. L'ancien colonisateur a aussi emporte ou detruit des infrastructures, du materiel et des medicaments. Le gouvernement guineen s'est alors tourne vers l'Union sovietique, qui est devenue le nouveau partenaire du developpement du pays en matiere d'industrie, d'agriculture et d'infrastructures. 🇬🇳 AN68 : Célébration de la fête Nationale guinéenne : le président Mamadi DOUMBOUYA passe en revue les troupes #GN68 #GN67 #GN66 #GN65 #Jeune #SimandouAcademy #Simandou2040 pic.twitter.com/QBEn7qKSWQ — Lamine BA ✨️ (@LamineBA_) October 2, 2026 Festivites a Conakry Pour cette occasion, des evenements festifs ont ete programmes dans la capitale guineenne, avec la presence de plusieurs delegations etrangeres et des presidents Alassane Ouattara, de Cote d'Ivoire, et Paul Kagame, du Rwanda, invites d'honneur de cette celebration. La journee a demarre par un moment de recueillement preside par le chef de l'etat, Mamadi Doumbouya, en presence de la premiere dame. Apres la ceremonie, le couple presidentiel a assiste au grand defile traditionnel, qui a reuni les neuf regions administratives du pays ainsi que les forces de defense et de securite.

items.title: UNDP invites Mahama Ayariga to Northern Peace Conference in Tamale
items.description: The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has invited the Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, to participate in the Northern Peace Conference scheduled for October 26 to 27, 2026, in Tamale. The two-day conference, to be held at the Global Dreams Hotel, is being organised by the UNDP in partnership with the Parliamentary Northern Caucus, the National Peace Council and the Northern Development Authority. In the invitation signed by UNDP Resident Representative Niloy Banerjee, the organisation said the conference would form part of ongoing efforts “to strengthen peacebuilding, social cohesion, and inclusive dialogue across Northern Ghana.” The UNDP said the conference would provide “a strategic platform for policymakers, traditional authorities, civil society actors, development partners, youth and women representatives, security institutions, and other key stakeholders” to reflect on emerging peace and security dynamics, share lessons from ongoing initiatives and identify practical pathways for sustaining peace and development in the region. The organisation further said Mr Ayariga’s participation would be valuable given the Ministry’s role in “advancing peace, strengthening social cohesion, and supporting Ghana’s sustainable development agenda.” It added that his “participation, perspectives and expertise will enrich the discussions and contribute significantly to shaping policy and programmatic actions” aimed at advancing peacebuilding and sustainable development outcomes in Northern Ghana. The Minister’s office has been asked to confirm his participation by October 7, 2026, with the UNDP indicating that a representative would follow up with the Ministry to address any questions or clarifications ahead of the conference.

items.title: Rentrée judiciaire 2026-2027 : ‎Le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ mise sur les valeurs endogènes pour une justice souveraine
items.description: Le Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, Garant de l’indépendance du Pouvoir judiciaire, a assisté dans la matinée de ce vendredi 02 octobre 2026, à l’audience solennelle de rentrée des cours et tribunaux du Burkina Faso, placée sous le thème : « Apport des mécanismes traditionnels de règlement des différends pour un meilleur accès à la justice au Burkina Faso ». ‎Ce thème s’inscrit directement dans la vision du Chef de l’État, engagé à intégrer les valeurs endogènes de gestion des conflits au cœur du système judiciaire national. Cette orientation stratégique s'est matérialisée par l’adoption, par l’Assemblée législative du Peuple, de la loi Faso Bu Kaoré, qui institutionnalise la justice traditionnelle. ‎Dans son discours à la Nation du 31 décembre 2025, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré avait précisé les fondements de cette démarche : « Nous ne pouvons pas importer une justice, l’appliquer telle quelle et espérer garantir la cohésion sociale. En intégrant nos valeurs ancestrales ainsi que les personnes-ressources dans la résolution de certains litiges, nous poserons les bases d’un espace de cohésion sociale solide et durable ». ‎À travers cette réforme, le Président du Faso entend bâtir une justice souveraine, accessible et véritablement ancrée dans le substrat socioculturel burkinabè. Sa présence à la Rentrée judiciaire marque son soutien aux acteurs du secteur de la justice pour la rendre plus accessible aux populations pour une meilleure cohésion sociale. ‎ ‎Direction de la communication de la Présidence du Faso
